svg.aria-label: How AWS Lake Formation actually enforces access: the four step credential vending flow from a principal through an integrated engine to the Data Catalog, Lake Formation and Amazon S3; the direct S3 path that bypasses all of it; the three states a Data Catalog resource can be in, which are AWS Glue resource governed by IAM alone, Lake Formation resource governed by Lake Formation permissions, and hybrid resource which switches per principal; and the arithmetic that makes tag based access control scale where named resource grants do not
svg.title: AWS Lake Formation does not sit in the Amazon S3 data path. It works by credential vending: a principal submits a query to an integrated engine such as Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue or Amazon Redshift Spectrum; the engine asks the AWS Glue Data Catalog for the table; the Data Catalog checks the principal’s Lake Formation permissions and returns only the metadata that principal is allowed to see; the catalog tells the engine whether the underlying location is registered with Lake Formation, and if it is, the engine asks Lake Formation for temporary credentials; the engine then reads Amazon S3 with those credentials and applies column, row or cell filtering itself before returning results. A principal that holds s3:GetObject on the bucket bypasses every step of this, because nothing asked Lake Formation anything. A Data Catalog resource can be in one of three states: an AWS Glue resource, which is not registered and where the IAMAllowedPrincipals group holds Super so access is decided entirely by IAM policies and the bucket policy; a Lake Formation resource, which is registered and enforced, where revoking IAMAllowedPrincipals is the moment enforcement begins and also the moment every job that relied on IAM alone stops working; and a hybrid resource, registered in hybrid access mode, which enforces only CREATE_TABLE, CREATE_PARTITION and UPDATE_TABLE by default, requires both Lake Formation and IAM permissions from opted in principals, and leaves everyone else working on IAM alone. Finally, the arithmetic: with the named resource method the number of grants required is the number of principals multiplied by the number of resources, so 200 principals and 900 tables is 180,000 grants, while with tag based access control using a single LF-Tag the total is the number of principals plus the number of resources, or 1,100 operations, and inheritance from database to table to column usually pushes the assignment count well below the table count.

g.text: Lake Formation is an authorisation plane, not a gate on the bucket
It only decides anything when an engine agrees to ask it, and only for locations that were registered.

2. The path that consults none of it — and it is the path most estates still use
A principal holding s3:GetObject on the bucket reads the Parquet directly.
No metadata call. No permission check. No credential vending. No column, row or cell filtering, because filtering is
something the engine does on the way out, and there is no engine in this path. Every grant you wrote is simply not consulted.
AWS puts it plainly: “If the table is not managed by Lake Formation, the second call from the analytic engine is made directly to Amazon S3.”

4. Why the tag model is the one that survives an estate of any size
Named resources cost n(P) x n(R) grants. LF-TBAC costs n(P) + n(R) operations.
180,000 grants to write, review and revoke
Tables inherit LF-Tags from databases and columns inherit from tables, and inherited values can be overridden. So in practice the
assignment count lands well below the table count: you tag the database once, not each of the forty tables inside it.
Quotas per Region: 30 data lake administrators, 1,000 LF-Tags per account, 1,000 values per LF-Tag, 10,000 registered paths.
